Install drip irrigation at soil level and avoid wetting foliage
Stake and prune tomato vines to promote airflow and rapid canopy drying
general_management: Remove and destroy severely infected localized plants promptly to prevent wider field infestation
Apply copper bactericide combined with mancozeb or bio-fungicide (Bacillus amyloliquefaciens) at first detection
Disinfect stakes, trellises, and pruning tools with a 10% bleach or sanitizing quaternary solution
Thoroughly clean up and plow under crop residue immediately after the final harvest
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.expert_guidance: Consult local agricultural extension for advice on copper-resistant bacterial strains and bacteriophage biocontrol options.

common_symptoms: Dark brown to black necrotic spots starting on older lower foliage
Distinctive concentric rings within lesions resembling a target or bullseye pattern
Surrounding leaf tissue turns yellow (chlorotic halo) and withers
Defoliation moves progressively upward from ground level, exposing fruit to sunscald
Dark, sunken, leathery lesions at the stem-end of ripening fruit
contributing_factors: Warm temperatures between 24°C and 29°C with prolonged humidity or rainfall
Rain splash transferring soil-borne fungal spores onto lower leaves
Plant stress caused by heavy fruit load, drought, or nitrogen deficiency
Dense, unpruned tomato foliage that stays wet for hours
prevention_practices: Prune off the bottom 30 cm of leaves once plants are established to eliminate soil contact
Apply 7-10 cm straw or plastic mulch around the plant base to prevent soil splash onto foliage
Practice 3-year crop rotation away from solanaceous plants (potatoes, peppers, eggplants)
Water exclusively with drip tape or soaker hoses at the soil line in the morning
Stake, cage, and trellis tomatoes to maintain upright, well-ventilated growth
general_management: Prune out infected lower leaves immediately upon first sighting; do not compost infected foliage
Apply registered preventive bio-fungicides (such as Bacillus subtilis or copper formulations) early in disease onset
Maintain balanced fertility to prevent plant stress during peak fruit set
Remove all vine debris at season end to prevent overwintering fungal spores
Tomato___Early_blight.expert_guidance: Contact local extension specialists for TOM-CAST disease forecasting values to time any protective treatments.

common_symptoms: Large, irregular, water-soaked pale green to dark brown oily lesions on leaves
White, frosty, velvety mold growth visible on leaf undersides during moist mornings
Dark brown to black greasy-looking cankers on stems and petioles
Rapid total collapse, shriveling, and browning of the entire plant canopy
Firm, greasy, golden-brown to dark brown rot on green or ripe tomato fruit
contributing_factors: Cool, wet, foggy, or overcast weather with temperatures between 15°C and 22°C
High relative humidity (>90%) with prolonged leaf wetness exceeding 8 hours
Airborne sporangia carried on storm winds for tens of miles
Nearby infected potato fields, volunteer potatoes, or cull piles
prevention_practices: Select late-blight-resistant tomato cultivars (e.g., Defiant Ph-R, Mountain Merit, Mountain Magic, Iron Lady)
Never compost infected plants or plant near unmanaged potato crops
Provide wide spacing (90-120 cm) between tomato plants to maximize canopy airflow
Monitor regional late blight tracking systems (USABlight / EuroBlight) weekly
general_management: CRITICAL: Late blight can destroy an entire tomato crop within 3 to 5 days
Immediately bag, cut down, and securely dispose of infected plants in trash bags; do not leave in open compost
Apply preventative copper or targeted systemic fungicides strictly prior to predicted rainfall when blight is reported in your region
Do not overhead water; keep foliage completely dry
Tomato___Late_blight.expert_guidance: MANDATORY: Notify your local agricultural extension service immediately if late blight is identified so neighboring growers can be alerted.

common_symptoms: Pale green to yellowish blotches with indistinct margins on upper leaf surfaces
Dense, velvety, olive-green to grayish-brown fungal sporulation on corresponding leaf undersides
Infected leaves curl, wither, turn golden brown, and drop prematurely
Predominantly affects older lower leaves first in high-tunnel or greenhouse crops
contributing_factors: High relative humidity (>85%) with moderate temperatures (21°C to 24°C)
Greenhouse, poly-tunnel, or sheltered high-density planting with poor ventilation
Overhead watering or condensation dripping from greenhouse plastic onto leaves
prevention_practices: Maximize ventilation in high tunnels and greenhouses with exhaust fans, ridge vents, and horizontal air fans
Maintain night temperatures slightly elevated to prevent dew and condensation formation on foliage
Space plants widely and prune lower suckers to open canopy airflow
Plant resistant tomato varieties possessing Cf resistance genes
general_management: Prune out infected lower leaves showing olive mold patches to reduce spore load
Water only at ground level early in the morning
Apply copper-based fungicides or bio-fungicides if humidity cannot be kept below 85%
Thoroughly sanitize greenhouse structures with disinfectant between planting cycles
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.expert_guidance: Check greenhouse environmental data loggers; keeping daytime/nighttime relative humidity below 80% effectively halts infection cycles.

common_symptoms: Numerous small (1.5 to 3 mm), circular spots starting on oldest lower foliage
Spots have dark brown borders and distinctly pale gray or tan circular centers
Tiny black specks (pycnidia fruiting bodies) clearly visible within the gray centers under magnification
Heavily infected leaves turn yellow, shrivel, and drop, resulting in progressive upward defoliation
contributing_factors: Moderate to warm temperatures (20°C to 27°C) accompanied by wet, rainy periods
Splashing water from rain or overhead sprinklers transferring spores from soil debris
Dense canopy where leaves touch wet soil
Weed hosts like horsenettle or jimsonweed growing near the field
prevention_practices: Mulch heavily around the base of plants (7-10 cm) immediately after transplanting to block soil splash
Prune lower foliage up to 30 cm from the ground once plants begin fruiting
Avoid overhead irrigation; use drip irrigation exclusively
Rotate crops on a 3-year cycle away from solanaceous plants
Eradicate nightshade and solanaceous weeds around garden perimeters
general_management: Remove and destroy infected leaves as soon as first spotted; do not compost
Apply protective fungicides (copper, chlorothalonil, or Bacillus-based products) starting at first sign and repeat according to label directions during wet weather
Stake plants securely to keep all vines upright
Clean and sanitize tomato stakes and cages at end of season
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.expert_guidance: Septoria primarily defoliates leaves and rarely affects fruit directly, but defoliation causes severe sunscald and reduces yield. Consult local extension for spray timing.

common_symptoms: Fine pale yellow, white, or bronze stippling / specks on upper leaf surfaces
Fine silken webbing spun on the undersides of leaves and across stem axils
Leaves turn chlorotic, bronze, dry, brittle, and drop prematurely
In severe infestations, whole tomato plants become enveloped in webbing and desiccate
contributing_factors: Hot, dry, dusty weather conditions (>27°C to 35°C with low humidity)
Broad-spectrum insecticide use that eliminates beneficial predatory mites and ladybugs
Water-stressed, drought-stressed plants
Dusty field borders along dirt roads
prevention_practices: Keep tomato plants well-hydrated; water-stressed plants are significantly more attractive to mites
Maintain dirt road wetting or windbreaks to minimize dust drift onto tomato rows
Avoid broad-spectrum pyrethroid insecticides that destroy natural predatory mite populations
Introduce or conserve biological control agents such as predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis, Neoseiulus californicus)
general_management: Spray strong jets of water onto leaf undersides to dislodge mites and destroy webbing in small plantings
Apply insecticidal soaps, horticultural oils, or neem oil, ensuring complete coverage of leaf undersides
Apply selective miticides only when economic thresholds are reached and rotate chemical classes to avoid resistance
Remove and destroy heavily webbed plants
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.expert_guidance: Use a 10x-20x hand lens to inspect the underside of stippled leaves to confirm live spider mites vs other pest feeding.

common_symptoms: Small water-soaked pinpoint spots on leaves expanding into circular brown lesions
Lesions show distinct concentric rings resembling targets, with pale brown centers and dark borders
Yellow halo often develops around mature lesions
Fruit lesions appear as deeply sunken, circular brown pits, often cracking open at the center
contributing_factors: Warm, humid conditions with temperatures between 24°C and 32°C
Overhead irrigation or prolonged dew periods (>10 hours)
Dense canopy with poor air movement and high leaf density
Volunteer plants and solanaceous weeds serving as spore reservoirs
prevention_practices: Plant tolerant varieties and ensure wide row spacing for optimal airflow
Use drip irrigation under mulch; strictly avoid wetting the foliage
Regularly prune suckers and lower canopy leaves to increase air movement
Rotate crops away from solanaceous plants, soybeans, and papayas for at least 2 years
general_management: Remove infected lower leaves promptly to prevent spore production
Apply protective fungicide sprays (copper formulations or azoxystrobin/difenoconazole) according to extension guidelines during warm wet weather
Clean up and bury all crop debris after harvest
Tomato___Target_Spot.expert_guidance: Distinguish carefully from Early Blight and Bacterial Spot; consult an extension diagnostic lab if uncertain.

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.pathogen: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus (TYLCV - Begomovirus, vectored by Silverleaf Whitefly)
common_symptoms: Marked upward curling and cupping of leaflet margins
Pronounced yellowing (chlorosis) along leaf margins and interveinal areas
Severe stunting and dwarfing of the entire plant with an erect, bushy appearance
Flowers frequently drop before setting fruit; fruit set is dramatically reduced or absent
contributing_factors: High populations of Silverleaf whitefly (Bemisia tabaci) insect vector
Warm to hot subtropical and tropical temperatures favoring rapid whitefly reproduction
Presence of alternate weed hosts (nightshades, mallow, weeds) in surrounding areas
Transport of asymptomatic infected transplants
prevention_practices: Plant TYLCV-resistant or tolerant tomato varieties (look for Ty-1, Ty-2, or Ty-3 gene resistance)
Install 50-mesh insect-proof netting in seedling production areas and high tunnels
Place yellow sticky cards around fields to monitor whitefly population levels
Use reflective silver mulches that repel whiteflies during early plant vegetative stages
Eliminate nightshade weeds and volunteer host plants within 150 meters of the planting area
general_management: Infected plants cannot be cured; rogue out and destroy infected plants immediately inside sealed plastic bags to prevent vector dispersal
Manage whitefly populations using insecticidal soaps, horticultural oils, or targeted systemic insecticides
Maintain a host-free fallow period between tomato crop cycles
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.expert_guidance: CRITICAL: TYLCV is a regulated plant virus in many agricultural regions. Contact your regional agricultural extension agent for whitefly resistance and vector management protocols.

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.pathogen: Tomato mosaic virus (ToMV - Tobamovirus, highly mechanically transmissible)
common_symptoms: Mottling of light green and dark green mosaic patterns on leaves
Leaf distortion: leaflets become narrow, elongated, crinkled, or strap-like ('fern-leaf' or shoestring)
Stunted plant growth and uneven ripening with internal brown browning of fruit walls
Yellowish blotches and bronze necrotic rings on ripening fruit
contributing_factors: Mechanical transmission via hands, pruning shears, trellis twine, and machinery
Tobacco use by greenhouse workers (virus can persist in manufactured tobacco products)
Infected seed or seed coats
Extreme stability: virus remains infective in dry plant debris and soil for years
prevention_practices: Plant certified virus-free seed treated with trisodium phosphate (TSP) or heat therapy
Select ToMV-resistant tomato varieties (designated 'Tm' or 'ToMV' resistant)
Require workers to wash hands thoroughly with soap and water before handling plants; ban tobacco use near crops
Dip tools in non-fat dry milk solution (20%) or 10% household bleach between pruning each plant
general_management: There is no chemical cure for viral infections in plants
Rogue out and destroy infected plants immediately upon visual identification; handle infected plants last
Do not touch adjacent healthy plants after handling infected plants
Discard stakes and trellising twine used on infected plants or steam sterilize
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.expert_guidance: Distinguish between ToMV and Cucumber Mosaic Virus (CMV) or Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus (TSWV) via ELISA or PCR laboratory testing through your extension plant pathology diagnostic clinic.

common_symptoms: Vigorous, deep green compound foliage with clean serrated margins
Firm, upright stems with glandular trichome hairs and natural tomato aroma
Abundant blossom clusters with bright yellow petals and complete pollination
Plump, symmetrical, smooth fruit without cracking, spots, or blossom end rot
contributing_factors: Full sun exposure (minimum 6-8 hours direct sunlight daily)
Well-drained loamy soil with pH between 6.2 and 6.8 rich in organic matter
Consistent moisture delivered via drip irrigation at soil level
Staking, trellising, or caging providing upright structural support
prevention_practices: Maintain 7-10 cm clean organic mulch (straw, untreated wood chips) around root zones
Prune lower foliage 30 cm from ground level once first cluster sets fruit to avoid soil splash
Scout weekly for early hornworm, aphid, or fungal spore appearance
Perform soil or petiole tests to balance calcium and nitrogen nutrition
general_management: No chemical disease treatment necessary
Maintain regular morning watering to prevent soil moisture swings and fruit splitting
Side-dress with balanced organic fertilizer as fruit load expands
Tomato___healthy.expert_guidance: Keep seasonal scouting logs tracking transplant dates, flowering, and first harvest to optimize crop rotation.
